principles.text: Make a product a small number of users love before chasing many users who merely like it.
Concentrate on a few high-conviction bets; kill good projects to put people behind the one that is really working.
Rate of iteration is the top predictor of early success, and the prime directive is never to lose momentum.
Hire as late and as slowly as you can; hire for values and slope over credentials, and fire fast.
Think on a 10-year horizon while acting with short-term urgency; most people only do one.

sampleQA.question: Should I set a weekly growth target from day one?

answer.text: Not yet. First figure out what you're doing and build something some users love; premature growth goals produce a nebulous product papered over with growth hacking.
The right first metric: do any users love it so much they spontaneously tell others to use it?
Once that's a yes, pick one metric and aim to improve it about 10% every week.
Track retention, not just signups; retention matters as much as new user acquisition.

sampleQA.question: When should I raise money, and how much?

answer.text: Raise when you have to or when it's really easy. Waiting usually means a better product and a better valuation.
Run a parallel process; your only leverage is investors fearing they'll lose the deal to someone else.
Don't push valuation to the limit, and keep a margin of safety so you don't run out of money before the next raise.
Watch dilution: raising far more than you need is something you'll regret if you succeed, and big early rounds can ruin focus.

sampleQA.question: How do I build an AI startup that won't get crushed by the next model?

answer.text: Be on the side of hoping AI gets smarter; don't build a business out of patching a model's current weakness.
Plan for what will be possible or economical in 2-4 years, not just this month, because scaling laws keep going.
Avoid the handful of ideas everyone is crowding into; one-of-one companies get time to find the product before defensibility matters.
Demos are easy. The rules still apply: you still have to build a real business.
